facts.text: On this date in 1938, Chamberlain returned from Munich declaring 'peace for our time.' Within a year, Britain was at war — making it one of history's most catastrophically wrong predictions.
On this date in 1829, London's Metropolitan Police Force was founded. It was so distrusted at first that officers were regularly pelted with rubbish by the public they were meant to protect.
More people live inside a 40km radius of Jakarta than in the entire country of Australia.
Mongolia has a lower population density than any sovereign nation on Earth — roughly 2 people per square kilometer — yet its capital, Ulaanbaatar, holds nearly half the country's entire population.
The United Arab Emirates imports nearly all of its food and over 90% of its water, making it one of the most resource-dependent nations on the planet despite sitting on vast oil wealth.

On this date in 1982, Tylenol's maker Johnson & Johnson pulled 31 million bottles from shelves after a poisoning scare — and its stock recovered within weeks. The crisis became a masterclass in how transparency can be a balance-sheet asset.
On this date in 2008, the U.S. House rejected the $700 billion TARP bailout bill, and the Dow fell 778 points — the largest single-day point drop in its history at the time.
The New York Stock Exchange was founded in 1792 under a buttonwood tree on Wall Street. The tree is gone; the trading floor itself may soon follow, as over 90% of NYSE volume is now electronic.
Saudi Aramco briefly became the first company to exceed a $2 trillion market cap in 2019 — a valuation larger than the entire GDP of Italy.
Warren Buffett's Berkshire Hathaway once traded for $8 a share. A single Class A share now costs more than $600,000, making it the most expensive stock on any major U.S. exchange by design.
On this day in 1901, Enrico Fermi was born. He built the first nuclear reactor beneath a Chicago squash court in 1942 and never told the university he was doing it.
On this day in 1988, NASA launched the Space Shuttle Discovery, its first mission after Challenger. The crew carried a single red apple — a quiet tribute to the seven who died.
A neutron star packs more mass than the Sun into a sphere the size of a city. A teaspoon of its material would weigh about a billion tons on Earth.
Your body replaces roughly 330 billion cells every day — about 3.8 million per second. You are, in the most literal sense, not the same person you were last year.
Quantum entanglement allows two particles to share states instantly across any distance, yet it cannot be used to send information faster than light — the universe found a loophole.
On this day in 1938, Chamberlain signed the Munich Agreement. He flew home by plane — a technology the Wright Brothers had only demonstrated to the U.S. Army 30 years earlier.
Oxford University was teaching students when the Aztec Empire didn't yet exist. Oxford: 1096. Aztecs: 1428.
On this day in 1829, London's Metropolitan Police held their first day of duty — making the world's first modern police force younger than the United States Constitution.
Cleopatra lived closer in time to the Moon landing than to the construction of the Great Pyramid. The pyramid: 2560 BC. Cleopatra: 69 BC. Apollo 11: 1969 AD.
The fax machine was patented in 1843 — before the American Civil War, before the telephone, and 140 years before most offices actually got one.
Sonder (n.): the realization that each passerby has a life as vivid and complex as your own. Coined by John Koenig in The Dictionary of Obscure Sorrows, 2012. Already feels ancient.
Vellichor (n.): the strange wistfulness of used bookshops. Also Koenig's invention — proof that a single person can will a word into meaning through sheer precision.
On this day in 1829, the London Metropolitan Police force was established, giving English the word 'bobby' — slang for founder Robert Peel, whose name now walks every British beat.
Hiraeth (n.): a Welsh longing for a home that may never have existed. Untranslatable because no other language thought to need it, which says something about Wales.
On September 29, 1758, Horatio Nelson was born, and with him the word 'nelsonian' — meaning a deliberate failure to see what is inconvenient — born from his famous blind-eye maneuver at Copenhagen.

On this date in 2022, Ethereum completed The Merge, switching from proof-of-work to proof-of-stake and cutting its energy use by ~99.95%. The transition happened with zero downtime on a live network holding $50B+ in assets.

On this date in 2021, El Salvador's Bitcoin Law had been in effect for 24 days — the first sovereign legal tender adoption of a cryptocurrency, making BTC legally equivalent to the US dollar for all debts.

Bitcoin's genesis block contains the text 'The Times 03/Jan/2009 Chancellor on brink of second bailout for banks' — hardcoded proof-of-timestamp and a quiet editorial, permanently embedded in every full node on earth.

The DAO hack of 2016 didn't exploit a flaw in Ethereum — it exploited a flaw in a Solidity contract's reentrancy logic. Ethereum itself worked exactly as designed, which is precisely why the community split over whether to reverse it.

Satoshi Nakamoto's known wallet addresses hold roughly 1.1 million BTC that has never moved — not one satoshi — across 17 years, through every boom, crisis, and legal pressure the ecosystem has faced.
On this date in 2009, ImageNet launched publicly — the 3.2-million-image dataset that would, three years later, ignite the deep learning era when AlexNet halved the benchmark error rate overnight.
Today in 2016, Google DeepMind's WaveNet paper dropped, generating raw audio waveforms sample-by-sample — 24,000 decisions per second of speech, each conditioned on all prior ones.
GPT-4's training run is estimated to have consumed more compute than all of humanity's combined AI research through 2012 — a field's entire pre-deep-learning history, compressed into one job.
Transformers have no built-in notion of word order. Position must be injected artificially — the architecture that now runs most of AI is, at its core, a permutation-invariant function.
Reinforcement learning from human feedback uses comparisons, not scores. Humans say which output is better, never how much — the entire alignment signal is ordinal, not cardinal.
